# F1 glossary

## Aerodynamics & car setup

**Downforce** — the aerodynamic force pushing a car down onto the track, generated by wings and the floor. More downforce means more grip in corners at the cost of top speed on straights.

**DRS (Drag Reduction System)** — a flap on the rear wing that opens to reduce drag on straights. A driver can only activate it when within one second of the car ahead at a detection point, and only inside designated DRS zones, from the third lap of the race onward (disabled for the first two laps and in wet or unsafe conditions).

**Parc fermé** — the period from the start of qualifying until the race begins, during which teams are barred from making significant setup changes to the car. Only very limited adjustments (like tyre pressures within a set range, or repairs) are allowed; anything more forces a driver to start from the pit lane.

**Ground effect** — downforce generated by shaping the underside of the car (the floor and diffuser) to accelerate airflow beneath it and create low pressure that sucks the car toward the track, rather than relying purely on wings. The current generation of F1 cars leans heavily on ground effect, a return to a principle banned for decades after it made 1980s cars dangerously sensitive to ride height changes.

**Porpoising** — a bouncing oscillation that afflicted ground-effect cars especially in 2022: the floor generates so much downforce that it sucks the car down until the floor stalls (airflow separates and downforce collapses), the car springs back up, the floor reattaches and generates downforce again, and the cycle repeats — visibly bouncing the car down the straights.

**Floor / diffuser** — the underside of the car and the upswept channel at its rear that manages airflow exiting from beneath it; both are central to how a modern F1 car generates most of its downforce (see ground effect).

**Front wing / rear wing** — the aerodynamic surfaces at the front and rear of the car, adjustable within regulation limits to balance the car's aerodynamic setup between front and rear grip.

**Dirty air / wake turbulence** — the disturbed, less dense air left behind a car, which reduces the downforce (and therefore grip) of any car following closely through it — a big part of why following, and therefore overtaking, is harder than driving in clean air.

**Slipstream / draft** — the reduced-drag pocket of air directly behind another car; tucking into it on a straight lets a following car reach a higher top speed, a factor in both qualifying (slipstreaming a teammate or rival) and race overtaking, especially combined with DRS.

**Halo** — the curved titanium bar surrounding the cockpit, mandated since 2018, designed to protect the driver's head from large flying debris or another car.

**Ballast** — weight added to the car (beyond what's structurally needed) specifically to help meet the minimum weight limit while letting the team choose where to place it, which shifts the car's weight distribution and can be used to fine-tune balance.

## Power unit

**Power unit** — the modern term for what used to just be called the engine: a 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrid combining the internal combustion engine (ICE) with hybrid electrical systems (see MGU-K and MGU-H) and their battery (the energy store).

**MGU-K (Motor Generator Unit – Kinetic)** — recovers kinetic energy under braking (like a road car's regenerative braking) and can deploy it back as extra power.

**MGU-H (Motor Generator Unit – Heat)** — recovers energy from the turbocharger's exhaust heat and either feeds it back into the electrical system or uses it to spin the turbo up, reducing turbo lag.

**Power unit penalty / grid penalty for components** — each driver is allotted a limited number of power unit components per season (engine, turbo, MGU-K, MGU-H, energy store, control electronics); fitting an additional one beyond the allowance costs a fixed number of grid-position places, applied at the next race.

## Tyres & strategy

**Undercut** — pitting earlier than a rival to get onto fresh tyres sooner, hoping the pace advantage of new rubber lets you pass them once they eventually pit themselves.

**Overcut** — the opposite: staying out longer than a rival on older tyres, gaining track position because your rival loses time in the pits while you keep circulating.

**Tyre degradation** — the rate at which a tyre loses grip and pace over a stint, caused by wear (rubber physically grinding away) and thermal degradation (overheating breaking down the rubber's structure).

**Graining / blistering** — two different tyre degradation failure modes. Graining happens when the tyre surface shears rather than grips, usually at lower temperatures; blistering is small pockets of gas forming under the surface at high temperatures. Both reduce grip.

**Stint** — the period a driver spends running on one set of tyres, from the moment they're fitted until the next pit stop (or the end of the session).

**Out-lap / in-lap** — the out-lap is the first lap after leaving the pits, run on cold tyres that haven't reached working temperature yet, so it's rarely a representative or fast lap; the in-lap is the final lap before pitting, often driven more cautiously to protect tyres or fuel that are no longer needed at full pace.

**Push lap / cool-down lap** — a push lap is a driver's maximum-effort attempt at a fast time; a cool-down (or "backing off") lap is deliberately slower, used to manage tyre and brake temperatures, especially between practice runs or after a fast qualifying lap.

## Timing & sessions

**FP1 / FP2 / FP3** — the three free practice sessions held before qualifying on a standard race weekend (a sprint weekend replaces FP2/FP3 with sprint qualifying and the sprint race instead).

**Q1 / Q2 / Q3** — the three knockout stages of a standard qualifying session. The slowest cars are eliminated after Q1 and Q2; the remaining ten fight for pole position in Q3.

**Gap vs. interval** — the "gap" is a driver's time behind the race leader; the "interval" is their time behind the car immediately ahead of them. Both are shown live during a race and update continuously as the field spreads out or bunches up.

**Delta (time)** — the time difference between two laps, sectors, or drivers — e.g. "purple" sector times (see below) are shown as a delta to the best time set so far.

**Purple sector / personal best** — during a session, the fastest sector or lap time set by ANY driver so far is highlighted purple on timing screens; a driver's own fastest sector or lap of the session (even if not the overall fastest) is highlighted green.

**Formation lap / reconnaissance lap** — the lap(s) before a standing start where the field circulates from the pit lane or grid to warm up tyres and brakes before lining up on the grid for the actual start.

## Race start & procedure

**Standing start** — the normal way an F1 race begins: cars line up stationary on the grid in their qualifying (or grid-penalty-adjusted) order and launch together at the five-red-lights-out signal.

**Rolling start** — used in some circumstances (e.g. after certain red-flag stoppages), where cars are already moving in formation when the race or restart begins, rather than launching from a standstill.

**Formation lap** — see above; also sometimes used loosely to mean the lap(s) run behind a safety car before a rolling restart.

**Box (box, box)** — the radio call telling a driver to pit ("box" being the team's term for the pit garage), typically repeated for clarity.

## Penalties & incidents

**Grid penalty** — a penalty (for a rules breach, or for exceeding a power unit component allocation) that moves a driver back a set number of places on the starting grid, applied after qualifying positions are set.

**Time penalty** — seconds added to a driver's total race time after the fact for a rules infringement (e.g. causing a collision), rather than a grid or in-race positional penalty.

**Drive-through penalty** — a penalty served during the race itself: the driver must enter the pit lane, drive through it at the pit-lane speed limit without stopping, and rejoin the race — costing time without requiring a full stop.

**Stop-go penalty** — a more severe in-race penalty: the driver must enter the pits and stop in their pit box for a fixed number of seconds (with no tyre change or work allowed) before rejoining.

**Track limits** — the defined edge of the circuit (usually the white line, sometimes a kerb); exceeding them (all four wheels beyond the line) while gaining an advantage — most commonly setting a faster lap time — typically has that lap time deleted, and repeated offenses in a race can escalate to a time penalty.

**DNF / DNS / DSQ** — "Did Not Finish" (retired during the session, often mechanical failure or a crash), "Did Not Start" (failed to take the start, e.g. a grid-formation problem), and "Disqualified" (excluded from the results entirely, typically for a technical infringement discovered after the session, such as a car failing post-race scrutineering).

## Race control & flags

**Blue flag** — shown to a driver about to be lapped, instructing them to let the faster car through; ignoring it repeatedly can result in a penalty.

**Yellow flag / double yellow** — a yellow flag warns of danger ahead and bans overtaking in that marshaling sector; a double yellow signals more severe danger and requires drivers to be prepared to stop if necessary.

**Red flag** — the session is stopped entirely, usually for a serious incident or unsafe conditions (heavy rain, a car in a dangerous position, etc.).

**Checkered flag** — the session or race has ended.

**Safety car (SC)** — a physical car deployed onto the track that bunches the whole field up behind it at reduced speed, used for serious incidents needing the track partially or fully controlled.

**Virtual safety car (VSC)** — a lighter-touch version of the above: no physical car appears, but all drivers must stay under a set delta time until it ends, used for less severe incidents.

## Qualifying & race formats

**Pole position** — the first grid slot for the race, earned by setting the fastest time in Q3 (or, if a driver doesn't reach Q3, the fastest achieved in whichever session they were eliminated in still sets their grid slot for that group).

**Podium** — the top three finishing positions in a race, and the trophy presentation ceremony held for them after the race.

**Sprint** — a shorter, standalone race held on the Saturday of select race weekends, awarding a reduced points scale to the top eight finishers, separate from the main Grand Prix.

**Drivers' Championship vs. Constructors' Championship** — the Drivers' Championship ranks individual drivers by points scored across the season; the Constructors' Championship ranks each TEAM by the combined points of both their drivers. A driver can only score for themselves; a team scores from both its cars, which is why constructors' standings and drivers' standings don't always tell the same story about who's "winning."

**Team radio** — the live communication channel between a driver and their race engineer/pit wall, used for strategy calls, warnings, and encouragement — broadcasters often air selected exchanges during a race.
